Abstract—The dynamically evolving and technologically-driven
hybrid landscape of transportation networks integrated with
advanced edge computing capabilities has demonstrated efficient
communication and computation techniques to guarantee robust
quality of services (QoS) to vehicles. However, conventional
communication systems in the Internet of Vehicles (IoV) still
encounter challenges in providing meaningful low-latency com-
munication and AI-assisted real-time synchronization on the
edge. One reason is that it has exhausted the Shannon limit
by utilizing cellular, NOMA, and Wi-Fi technologies. Therefore,
we present an integrated approach leveraging Semantic Commu-
nication (SC), and Digital Twin (DT) deployment to tackle the
challenges caused by high-dimensional data exchanges and re-
source spectrum crunch leading to inevitable latency constraints.
SC stimulates meaningful transmission of data to high-mobility
vehicles by providing a relevant knowledge base (KB) and DT
deployment. In this paper, we established the vehicular SC (VSC)
model, and DT deployment strategy. We formulate a multi-
objective optimization problem (MOP) to maximize the overall
QoS of the system by jointly optimizing VSC and DT deployment.
Compared to traditional deep-reinforcement learning (DRL)
schemes, we propose a Digital Twin Semantic Sensing using the
Multi-vehicle DRL (DTS2-MVDL) algorithm which addresses
the MOP and persistent issues of multi-dimensional, continuous,
and discrete nature of the vehicular environment. Lastly, we
employ age of Information (AoI), latency, and QoS as the
performance metrics to determine the algorithmic efficiency.
Index Terms—Semantic communication, Digital Twin, Dy-
namic optimization, Internet of Vehicles (IoV), Service optimiza-
tion

portation System (ITS) lacks real-time sensing capabilities
and continuous data engagement with the edge servers (ES)
limiting the smooth functioning of AI-based tasks such as
traffic forecast, path planning, cruise control, etc., [2]. Digital
twin (DT) plays an important role in providing real-time
virtual support for the physical activities happening on the
roads. It requires physical data of the IoV space to deliver
seamless support across the geographical regions through
which the vehicles are moving. Currently, the sensing data
is derived from the onboard sensors installed in the Intelligent
Connected Vehicles (ICVs), but it is difficult to collate massive
data coming from different vehicles and operate on it. It is
because of the different sensing abilities of many vehicles and
the interference of the ambient environmental adversities, the
sensing data gets affected. This also disturbs the precision of
the DT data collection process.
In addition, the optimal DT deployment remains a vexed
question that requires further exploration. Since edge com-
puting delivers low-latency services to vehicles, DTs can be
deployed on the ESs installed across the roads. However, due
to the frequent vehicle mobility, the DT dynamically migrates
itself according to the change in the location of the vehicle
incurring heavy transmission costs. Therefore, a strategy to
optimize the DT deployment is required based on the network
service availability and varied migration needs, which poses
another challenge [3]. Further, in order to achieve maximum
communication, IoVs transmit loads of data to the network
resources inflicting issues like overprovisioning, mismanage-
ment, breach of privacy, energy misuse, etc. Consequently,
efficient communication and computation should be advocated
to deliver better QoS.
Therefore, we utilize a transformative paradigm called
Vehicular Semantic Communication (VSC) which facilitates
meaningful communication between the traffic entities. It
has been standardized after the existing traditional Shannon
paradigm for better transmission reliability [4], [5], [6], [7].
For instance, an SC-facilitated sender vehicle utilizes the back-
ground knowledge base (KB) pertinent to the source messages
for retrieving relevant content and retains the semantic data
which requires only fewer bits to get transmitted. This process
is recognized as semantic encoding [5]. After the vehicle at
the receiving end gets equipped with the same information as
the sender, the onboard semantic engine retrieves the actual
knowledge from the received information ignoring the bit


2
errors. This sequence of actions is called semantic decoding
[5]. In fact, the driving logic behind the surge in the interest
of VSC is due to its ability to accurately represent semantic
knowledge and generalize well to real-world nuances. In
addition, with semantic assistance for the SOTA DNN mod-
els, they can provide multimodal services, including solving
IoV issues. VSC aids the network infrastructure in getting
engaged not only in active communication but also evolve
itself to execute intelligent task-oriented transmissions. It also
preserves bandwidth, reduces latency, and encourages other
network enhancements. Leveraging VSC in IoV, the collabora-
tive sensing in vehicles can be established for achieving better
V2X connectivity and realize driving tasks collectively. When
the vehicles are semantically oriented to send and decode the
transmitted knowledge, it will lead to cooperative tasks such as
perception, platooning etc., to form an integrated ecosystem.
Since the mobility of the vehicles, different offloading task
requirements, data scheduling, and variational environment
strains the VSC process, Deep-reinforcement learning (DRL)
techniques have emerged as a working solution for intelligent
interaction and for many AI-based tasks driving the vehi-
cles. It caters to resource spectrum scarcity and recognizes
dynamic environments in the IoV domain to design optimal
policies. By dynamically learning the environmental changes,
DRL empowers the vehicles with optimal sensing and DT
deployment intelligence. As a pivotal feature in vehicular
communication, IoV often ignores the fluctuating territory
problem and moves out of the ES communication range
aggravating the straggler effect [8]. Given the drawbacks, it
is vital to jointly optimize the efficient sensing process i.e.,
VSC and DT configuration scheme for QoS optimization of
the system. [9]. In this paper, we first describe the IoV scenario
where VSC takes place, followed by the vehicle’s integrated
sensing and VSC process. Further, DT comes into play for the
synchronization of the physical processes. To solve the latency
constraint, we also introduce two important metrics i.e., Age
of Information (AoI) and QoS to characterize the recency of
the VSC happening between vehicles through DT and measure
the system efficiency respectively [4]. At the same time, we
also reflect on the performance of DT transmission in high-
speed vehicle mobility environments. To this end, we list our
contributions as follows:
• To promote an integrated environment facilitating low-
latency VSC and real-time updates for the vehicles, we
develop a DT-enabled framework with a three-layered
architecture. The physical layer has ICVs uploading their
contextual data on edge where DTs are intelligently con-
figured. To support compute-intensive AI model training
and other traffic administrative analytics, DTs interact
with the base layer and deliver traffic assistance on roads.
• To address the spectrum shortage, we propose a VSC
model and DT deployment strategy to utilize the se-
mantics of the communication i.e., location, trajectory,
vehicle-edge connection, etc., and synchronize the latest
information passed by the vehicles to the DT on edge.
• To solve the multi-optimization problem (MOP), we
jointly optimize integrated sensing and DT deployment
through the VSC model and DT migration model to
maximize the system QoS. We design an algorithm
called Digital Twin Semantic Sensing using Multi-vehicle
Deep-reinforcement Learning (DTS2-MVDL) to solve
the MOP.
• Lastly, to measure the performance of the proposed
framework, we utilize AoI and QoS as the performance
metrics. Alongside this, the DT transmission cost is also
analyzed and compared with different baseline schemes.
Additionally, the proposed framework is compared with
the other existing learning schemes to prove its superior-
ity.
II. SYSTEM MODEL
This section describes an integrated framework of the DT-
empowered VSC model. Each vehicle is capable of doing
SC with each other and comes within the coverage range
of different ESs spread across various geographical regions.
The vehicles pair with the area’s respective ES for its services
forming a vehicle-service pair. The ES plays the role of SC
service providers which provision the stochastic vehicular re-
quests requiring information [10]. The DT deployed on the ES
keeps the state information of all the operating vehicles falling
within its coverage. The vehicle mobility strictly follows a
Poisson distribution over a multiple time intervals. Let us
assume that the model operates in a discrete-time interval,
represented as T = {0, 1, ...t, t + 1}. We consider τ as the
duration for every time slice t ∈T, (given ≪t), i.e., t is
significantly small [11], [12].

C. Realistic Fading Effects in Vehicular Sensing
We also evaluate the SC performance by considering three
realistic fading effects: Rayleigh, Rician, and Nakagami [14].
We address the real-time interferences with the intention to
thoroughly examine the VSC process with the unique char-
acteristics of each effect. Rayleigh fading is a conventional
model that assumes the absence of a direct line-of-sight (LOS),
making it suitable for environments with extensive multipath
propagation. Rician fading builds upon the Rayleigh model
by incorporating an element of LOS in conjunction with the
scattered signals, while Nakagami serves as a combination
effect that encompasses both Rayleigh and Rician effects. This
effect offers greater adaptability for capturing diverse propa-
gation scenarios. Further, our evaluation section also focuses
on additional performance metrics, emphasizing on effective

In DT-enabled IoV, wireless communication between ve-

Loss model establishes a reference point to estimate signal
attenuation based on the spatial separation between the trans-
mitter vehicle and receiver vehicle. Governed by the inverse
square law, the signal strength at the receiver side diminishes
inversely to the square of the distance between the source and
receiver. This model serves as a fundamental reference point
for analyzing signal propagation in unobstructed scenarios and
is frequently utilized as a benchmark for evaluating advanced
propagation models in IoV simulations [17].
Shadowing Models: It addresses large-scale signal fluctua-
tions caused by physical obstructions such as network infras-
tructure, vehicles, terrain, and other environmental elements,
that are critical to coverage patterns and network connectivity.
We employ Log-Normal Shadowing Model in this analysis to
account for these variations.
Log-Normal Shadowing Model: The Log-Normal Shadow-
ing Model is a widely adopted model in IoVs, designed to
simulate signal attenuation due to environmental obstructions
and terrain irregularities. It postulates that the received signal
power strictly adheres to a Log-Normal distribution. As ve-
hicles navigate the heterogeneous environments with diverse
obstruction levels, the Log-Normal Shadowing Model provides
a more accurate characterization of signal diminishing effect.
By integrating shadowing element into propagation modelling,
this approach boosts the fidelity of IoV simulations, facilitat-
ing the optimization of the proposed VSC scenario and DT
deployment strategy to maintain robust communication within
ITS.

For solving MOP, we provide an optimized solution called

balance in the training process. During the execution phase,

from other agents.

Abstract: The dynamically evolving and technologically-driven hybrid landscape of transportation networks integrated with advanced edge computing capabilities has demonstrated efficient communication and computation techniques to guarantee robust quality of services (QoS) to vehicles. However, conventional communication systems in the Internet of Vehicles (IoV) still encounter challenges in providing meaningful low-latency com- munication and AI-assisted real-time synchronization on the edge. One reason is that it has exhausted the Shannon limit by utilizing cellular, NOMA, and Wi-Fi technologies. Therefore, we present an integrated approach leveraging Semantic Commu- nication (SC), and Digital Twin (DT) deployment to tackle the challenges caused by high-dimensional data exchanges and re- source spectrum crunch leading to inevitable latency constraints. SC stimulates meaningful transmission of data to high-mobility vehicles by providing a relevant knowledge base (KB) and DT deployment. In this paper, we established the vehicular SC (VSC) model, and DT deployment strategy. We formulate a multi- objective optimization problem (MOP) to maximize the overall QoS of the system by jointly optimizing VSC and DT deployment. Compared to traditional deep-reinforcement learning (DRL) schemes, we propose a Digital Twin Semantic Sensing using the Multi-vehicle DRL (DTS2-MVDL) algorithm which addresses the MOP and persistent issues of multi-dimensional, continuous, and discrete nature of the vehicular environment. Lastly, we employ age of Information (AoI), latency, and QoS as the performance metrics to determine the algorithmic efficiency.
